items.title: A maximal algebraically independent set is a transcendence basis
items.strategy: For an element beta outside a maximal algebraically independent set A, a polynomial relation on A union {beta} must involve beta; read it as a nonzero polynomial in beta with coefficients in k[A] and divide by its leading coefficient in k(A) to make beta algebraic over k(A).

items.title: One element of a transcendence basis can be exchanged for a suitable rival
items.strategy: Let s lie in one transcendence basis S and write s as algebraic over the field generated by a second basis T. Choose a minimal finite subset of T occurring in such a relation and use that minimality to replace one of its elements by s while preserving algebraic independence and algebraicity of the ambient field.

items.title: Transcendence degree is additive in finite towers
items.strategy: Choose a transcendence basis of K over k and one of L over K. Their union is algebraically independent over k and generates a subfield over which L is algebraic, and exchange compares its size with any transcendence basis of L over k.

items.title: Over an infinite field, a triangular change makes a nonzero polynomial monic
items.strategy: Take the top homogeneous part H of the polynomial, choose scalars where H does not vanish, and rewrite after the triangular linear change x_i mapsto x_i + a_i x_n so the x_n-leading coefficient is a nonzero scalar.

items.title: Rapidly increasing power substitutions isolate one highest x_n-term
items.strategy: Substitute x_i + x_n^(N_i) with rapidly increasing weights. Base-expansion uniqueness makes one selected term contribute the unique highest power of x_n, so the transformed polynomial is essentially monic in x_n.

items.title: A monic relation makes the last generator integral over the earlier ones
items.strategy: Interpret the transformed relation in the quotient algebra. Once the last generator satisfies a monic polynomial over the subalgebra generated by the others, it is integral over that subalgebra.

items.title: Induction produces a polynomial subalgebra over which the affine algebra is integral
items.strategy: Induct on the number of algebra generators. If they are algebraically independent, stop; otherwise use the infinite-field or finite-field monic substitution to make one generator integral over the transformed subalgebra on the others, apply the induction hypothesis downstairs, and finish by transitivity of integrality.

items.title: Noether normalisation yields module finiteness over a polynomial subring
items.strategy: Once the affine algebra is integral over a polynomial subalgebra generated by finitely many elements, invoke the finite-generator module-finiteness theorem.

items.title: A domain finite over a polynomial ring has dimension at least the number of variables
items.strategy: Lift the standard prime chain (0) subset (x_1) subset (x_1, x_2) subset ... subset (x_1, ..., x_d) from the polynomial subring through the integral extension.

items.title: The rational function field k(t) is not finite over k[t]
items.strategy: If finitely many rational functions generated k(t) over k[t], only finitely many irreducible polynomials could appear in their denominators. The inverse of a new irreducible cannot lie in the generated module.

items.title: A finitely localized polynomial ring in positive dimension is not a field
items.strategy: Choose a one-variable specialization that keeps the finite denominator product nonzero, view the localized ring inside a rational function field in one variable, and apply the previous denominator obstruction.

items.title: A finite-type field reduces to a localization over a transcendence basis
items.strategy: Choose a finite transcendence basis t_1, ..., t_r of the field over k. Every remaining algebra generator is algebraic over k(t_1, ..., t_r), so after clearing finitely many denominators it becomes integral over a localization of k[t_1, ..., t_r].

items.title: A field finitely generated as a k-algebra is a finite extension of k
items.strategy: A nonempty transcendence basis would make the field integral over a finitely localized polynomial ring in positive transcendence degree, but such a localization is not a field. Therefore the transcendence basis is empty, and the field is finitely generated algebraic over k.

items.title: A maximal ideal of an affine algebra has finite residue field over the base field
items.strategy: Quotient the affine algebra by a maximal ideal. The quotient is both a field and a finitely generated k-algebra, so the field-form Zariski lemma makes it finite over k.

items.title: Evaluation at a point has kernel (x_1-a_1, ..., x_n-a_n)
items.strategy: Use monic division successively by x_n - a_n down to x_1 - a_1 to show every polynomial differs from its value at a by an element of the displayed ideal. The quotient is therefore the base field.

items.title: Over an algebraically closed field, every maximal ideal is an evaluation ideal
items.strategy: For a maximal ideal m, the residue classes of the coordinates live in the finite field extension k[x_1, ..., x_n]/m over k. Algebraic closedness forces that residue field to be k, and the previous lemma identifies m with the corresponding evaluation ideal.

items.title: The Rabinowitsch auxiliary ideal has no common zero
items.strategy: A common zero of I and 1 - yf would project to a point of V(I) where f vanishes, contradicting yf = 1.

items.title: The auxiliary ideal is the unit ideal
items.strategy: If the auxiliary ideal were proper, it would lie in a maximal ideal. Weak Nullstellensatz would realize that maximal ideal as an evaluation ideal, giving the forbidden common zero.

items.title: Substituting y = 1/f and clearing denominators yields a power of f in I
items.strategy: Work in the localization at the powers of f so that y may be replaced by f^(-1). The resulting identity has only finitely many denominators, and one power of f clears them all.

items.title: Strong Nullstellensatz: I(V(I)) equals the radical of I
items.strategy: One inclusion is pointwise: if f^N lies in I and every point annihilates I, then f vanishes there too. For the converse, apply the three Rabinowitsch lemmas to the vanishing hypothesis on f.

items.title: k-points of k[x_1, ..., x_n]/I are exactly k-algebra maps to k
items.strategy: A k-algebra map out of k[x_1, ..., x_n]/I is determined by the images of the coordinate classes, and it factors exactly when every generator of I vanishes at that tuple.

items.title: Over an algebraically closed field, maximal ideals of an affine algebra are kernels of points
items.strategy: Maximal ideals of the quotient algebra correspond to maximal ideals in a polynomial presentation modulo I, and weak Nullstellensatz turns those into evaluation kernels. The previous lemma translates them into k-points.

items.title: A vanishing ideal is always radical
items.strategy: If f^N vanishes at every point of a subset X, then in each residue field value f(x) has Nth power zero and hence is zero.

items.title: An ideal and its radical have the same zero locus
items.strategy: Every element of the radical has a power in the ideal, and powers have the same pointwise zeros over a field.

items.title: A radical ideal can be separated from an outside element by a point
items.strategy: Lift the radical ideal in the affine algebra to a radical ideal in a polynomial presentation. If no k-point killed the ideal while keeping f nonzero, strong Nullstellensatz would force f into that radical ideal.

items.title: A ring is Jacobson exactly when every prime is an intersection of maximal ideals above it
items.strategy: One direction specializes the Jacobson condition from radical ideals to prime ideals. The other writes a radical ideal as an intersection of containing primes and then replaces each prime by the intersection of the maximal ideals above it.

items.title: Finite-type maps from Jacobson rings induce finite residue-field extensions at maximal ideals
items.strategy: Localize the finite-type map at the contraction of a maximal ideal. The induced map on residue fields is again of finite type, so Zariski's lemma over the residue field of the base prime makes the upper residue field finite over it.

items.title: In a finite-type algebra over a field, radical ideals are intersections of maximal ideals
items.strategy: Quotient by the radical ideal and use the Jacobson criterion on the reduced finite-type algebra. For a nonzero element f, choose a maximal ideal in the localization at f; the residue-field lemma forces its contraction back to the quotient to be maximal and to avoid f.

items.title: A transcendence basis of k(s, t, sqrt(s+t)) over k
items.strategy: Use s and t as an algebraically independent pair and verify that sqrt(s+t) is algebraic over k(s, t) by its quadratic equation.

items.title: A triangular change makes a bivariate relation monic
items.strategy: Apply the infinite-field triangular substitution to a concrete polynomial, read off the new monic relation in the chosen variable, and identify the resulting finite polynomial subring.

items.title: Finite-field normalization needs the weight trick
items.strategy: Use the explicit F_q example where no linear change works, then apply the rapid-exponent substitution and check that one x_n-power becomes uniquely highest.

items.title: A new irreducible denominator stays outside a finitely generated subalgebra of k(t)
items.strategy: List the irreducible factors that appear in the denominators of the chosen generators and exhibit the inverse of a fresh irreducible polynomial that cannot be produced from them.

items.title: Over R, not every maximal ideal is an evaluation ideal
items.strategy: Compare the evaluation ideal (x-a) with the maximal ideal (x^2+1), whose residue field is C rather than R.

items.title: I(V(x^2, xy)) keeps only the radical information
items.strategy: Compute the common zero set, identify its vanishing ideal directly, and compare it with the original nonradical ideal.

items.title: A small Rabinowitsch identity written out completely
items.strategy: Form the auxiliary ideal for a concrete vanishing problem, write an explicit unit-ideal identity in the enlarged polynomial ring, and clear the denominator after substituting y = 1/f.
